• Common name: Dwarf hygrophila
  • Other names: Dwarf hygro, Miramar weed, Indian weed, East Indian hygrophila, Indian swampweed
  • Difficulty: Moderate
  • Lighting: Moderate to high
  • pH: 5.0–7.0
  • GH: 2–15
  • Temperature: 22–28°C (71–82°F)
  • Substrate: Nutrient-rich
  • Can be grown emersed: Yes
  • Growth rate: Fast
  • Placement: Midground and background
  • Height: 25–50 cm
  • Propagation: By cuttings
  • Colour: Green to reddish

Hygrophila polysperma is a prohibited species in Florida, listed by the Florida Exotic Pest Plant Council as one of the most invasive non-indigenous aquatic plants. By forming dense submerged mats, it impedes water flow, clogs irrigation pumps and displaces native vegetation.

It is listed as a medicinal plant in the Indian states of West Bengal and Karnataka, where it is used for hemiplegia, stiff neck, facial paralysis and headache.

Hygrophila polysperma 'White' is a special selection developed in the Tropica greenhouses in Denmark. Grown above water, the plant is light green and may show small spikes on the leaves. Once planted under water, it develops a striking pale green and white pattern.

Dwarf hygrophila is native to tropical and subtropical regions of India and Malaysia, from where it gradually spread to countries such as Cambodia, China, Laos, Myanmar, Nepal, Pakistan, Taiwan, Thailand and Vietnam.

In 1945 it was introduced to the US states of Texas, Florida and Virginia as Eastern Ludwiga. Over time it has adapted and naturalized in Florida and Texas, established itself in Kentucky and lakes in Virginia, and is present in northern Mexico.

Nowadays it is also present in thermally heated waters (uncharacteristic of natural conditions) in Austria, Germany, Hungary and Poland.

This plant grows emersed or submersed in stagnant water (ponds, lakes, marshes and rice fields) and in slow and fast-moving warm waters, or as a terrestrial plant in saturated soils. It usually grows at depths of 0.3–1.5 m.

Because of its size and fast growth, dwarf hygrophila is used as a background or midground plant, so a tank of 80 litres (20 gallons) or larger is recommended. If its growth is controlled by regular pruning, it can be kept in smaller aquariums, such as 40 litres (10 gallons).

In aquariums this plant is used as a classic stem plant, planted in dense groups along the sides and in the background because of its larger size. Under optimal conditions growth is fast, and it may take only a few weeks before it is ready for propagation or trimming. In nature it is invasive because it grows rapidly, multiplying its population tenfold in a year.

Trimming

Do not let the plant reach the surface, or you may get a big tangled mass. Start trimming when there are 10–15 cm left to the water surface. You can safely shorten it by half; it will grow back quickly. Trim regularly to prevent overcrowding and promote bushier growth.

Planting

Plant with about 5 cm between each stem and make sure it does not shade other plants. Plant it deep enough in the substrate to keep it from floating up; there is no special technique. Tips: use tweezers. Unlike some plants, it should not be left floating until roots develop.

Propagation

It propagates by shoots growing directly from leaf tips (under optimal conditions) and mainly by vegetative propagation through cuttings. Sometimes even detached leaves or fragments root and develop into new plants.

Cut the upper portion of the stem with sharp scissors, ideally about 10 cm long. Make a hole 3–4 cm deep in the substrate, place the stems gently in it and cover with substrate. In 7–10 days healthy stems develop roots and grow into new plants.

The plant grows upright with good branching, and regular trimming will encourage a compact and dense appearance. It is slow growing and adapts well to a wide range of conditions. Good lighting enhances the white patterning and keeps the growth compact.

The plant tolerates a wide range of water parameters, which is why it is considered invasive in some states.

Temperature: grows best at 22–28°C (71–82°F), with a minimum of 4°C (39°F). In Virginia it was documented tolerating freezing temperatures for brief periods. In New Zealand, however, it did not survive winter even without freezing water temperatures.

pH: prefers and grows best at pH 6.0–7.0. Experiments showed it can also tolerate pH 4.0–10.0; after 3 weeks all plants showed 100% survival at all pH levels.

Hardness: grows in soft and hard water, GH 2–15, but it grows faster in soft water.

Lighting

Requires medium-high light (30–50 PAR) with a standard photoperiod of 10–12 hours daily. It is very light-demanding, and strong light gives the best growth; the top leaves turn pinkish or reddish under sufficiently bright light. It does not tolerate long-term shading: with insufficient light the stem elongates, becomes leggy and density decreases.

Flow

No special requirements. The plant does well in still water or strong currents.

Substrate

Thrives in nutrient-rich substrates and is a very heavy root feeder. Substrate depth should be at least 2.5–5 cm. Recommended substrates include ADA Amazonia aqua soil, Carib Sea Eco-Complete and Seachem Fluorite.

CO2 and fertilization

CO2: technically it can be grown without CO2, but growth is much slower, less bushy and lacks a red tint. Under high light the tank must be balanced in CO2 and nutrients, otherwise it will be covered with algae quickly. Liquid carbon or (preferably) a pressurized CO2 system (20–30 mg/l) is recommended.

Fertilization: although a versatile feeder, it absorbs most nutrients through the roots (substrate). In its natural habitat the substrate has a particularly high concentration of phosphates and ammonia-nitrogen. Regular doses of liquid fertilizer (2–3 times a week) and root tabs (periodically) are recommended. Macro and micronutrients help sustain healthy growth and the best coloration.

If you keep shrimp in the tank, note that high CO2 levels and copper (present in most fertilizers) are extremely dangerous to shrimp.

Description

With its bushy foliage, Hygrophila polysperma makes an impressive background plant.

  • Growth habit: herbaceous rhizomatous perennial, rooted aquatic plant.
  • Growth form: can be grown emersed (paludarium) or fully submersed (aquarium). In nature it usually grows waterlogged.
  • Size: in aquariums usually 25–50+ cm tall. In nature stems reach up to 2 m.
  • Stem: creeping, ascending or erect, 1.5–2.2 mm in diameter, often prostrate, 4-angled and slightly swollen above the nodes.
  • Leaves: hairless, opposite and variable in size; submerged leaves are larger than emerged ones. Submerged leaves are long and narrow with a round or slightly pointed tip, 8–13 mm wide and 25–48 mm long. Emergent leaves are oblong to elliptical with a round tip, 5–10 mm wide and 12–45 mm long.
  • Colour: green, but under strong light it can get a yellowish or pink tint, most intense at the back of the leaf blade.
  • Flower: white with a blue tinge, about 5 mm long. The fruit is a small thin oval capsule, 5.5–8 mm, containing 20–30 seeds about 1 × 0.5 mm each.
  • Roots: well developed; adventitious roots form at the stem nodes.

Etymology

The genus name "Hygrophila" comes from the Greek "hygros" (moist) and "philos" (loving). The species name "polysperma" is also Greek, meaning "many seed".

Problems

  • Fragile: stems are brittle and break easily. Be careful when trimming and handling.
  • Ugly roots: adventitious roots form at the nodes. They cannot be fully avoided, so trim them.
  • Leggy: when the stem reaches the surface, the lower leaves are often shed, leaving a bare stem with lush foliage on top. Trim it or place it behind driftwood or rocks.
  • Overgrowth: under high light and CO2 it can fill the tank within weeks and needs regular trimming.
  • Relocation: the root system is well developed, so do not simply pull the plant out; be extra careful.

Quarantine

Unless the plant was grown in sterile/laboratory conditions (in vitro) and the pot is undamaged and unopened, quarantine and disinfect it first. Do not introduce a new plant to the tank straight after buying it.

  • The plant can carry parasites, pests such as snails, or even predators (dragonfly and damselfly nymphs, etc.).
  • It may contain residues of chemicals (pesticides) used against parasites and snails, which are extremely poisonous to fish, shrimp and other invertebrates.

Conclusion

Hygrophila polysperma is an attractive, decorative aquarium plant and an excellent choice for creating a tropical atmosphere. It is not for complete beginners, but is relatively easy to grow when its requirements are met: proper lighting, suitable temperature and a nutrient-rich substrate.

Its fresh, light tones create contrast among darker green or red plants and help brighten the overall layout. An excellent choice for midground or background placement, especially in layouts where contrast and texture play an important role.
